title: The desert, Luke's way (Luke 4:1–13)
hookLine: full of the Spirit, led into the wilderness, and the devil leaves until an opportune time
last: SON OF ADAM, SON OF GOD.

lines: DAY FORTY IS THE DANGEROUS DAY.
FULL OF THE SPIRIT, LED INTO THE WILDERNESS.
cards: Anyone who has quit something knows the dangerous moment isn't always the first day. It's day forty. You've made it.
You're proud. You're tired. And then the old thing shows up, sounding perfectly reasonable.
Luke's wilderness story begins, in the King James Bible: "Jesus being full of the Holy Ghost returned from Jordan, and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness."
Full of the Spirit, and led straight into the hardest place. Forty days without food. And Luke says, with almost comic plainness, "when they were ended, he afterward hungered."

teach.b: The devil makes three offers, each aimed at something real. First, hunger: "If thou be the Son of God, command this stone that it be made bread."
Jesus answers from Deuteronomy: "It is written, That man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God."

Second, power: all the kingdoms of the world, shown in a moment, if he will only worship. He refuses. Third, Luke takes him to Jerusalem, to a high point of the temple: throw yourself down, the angels will catch you.
This time the devil quotes scripture too, a psalm about angels bearing you up. Jesus answers: "It is said, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God." Here's Luke's way.
Matthew tells the same three tests but puts the mountain last.
Luke puts Jerusalem last. That's no accident: Luke's whole Gospel walks toward Jerusalem. It opened there, with Zechariah in the temple, and it will end there.
Then the line that gives today its name: "And when the devil had ended all the temptation, he departed from him for a season."
The Greek is achri kairou, until an opportune time. Not gone forever.

teach.h: HE DEPARTED FROM HIM FOR A SEASON.
teach.b: Just waiting. Readers often see that time return near the end, when Luke says Satan entered into Judas, and in the garden, where Jesus prays in agony.
Christians have long read this as honest news: passing one test doesn't end the testing. Temptation keeps a calendar.

how: Many churches read the temptation in the wilderness on the first Sunday of Lent, and the forty days of Lent are often linked to Jesus' forty days in the desert.

games.q: you've eaten nothing for forty days. a voice says: if you're the Son of God, make this stone bread. what do you do?
o: answer from scripture: man shall not live by bread alone.
ignore the voice and keep walking.
games.why: Jesus answers each test with words from Deuteronomy, and the devil leaves, but only until another time.

practice: Walk through an ordinary day in your mind and find your weakest hour, late at night with the phone, right after a hard meeting, hungry, tired, alone, bored, the way you'd find a weak board in a floor, without scolding yourself.

Then picture one small thing set there ahead of time: a glass of water, a walk, a verse, a friend to text, the phone in another room. If you pray, name that hour to God; if not, simply name it to yourself.

wordCard.voice: The desert. In Luke, Jesus goes in full of the Spirit, answers three tests with scripture, and the devil leaves only until an opportune time.

orig.note: Greek: the right time, the opportune moment. the devil leaves achri kairou, until such a time.

carryVoice: Your line: until another time. Full of the Spirit, and still tested. Day five hundred fifteen, done.
